title: Your rule, rewritten
hookLine: rewrite your three-line rule from this block's start
tomorrow: two weeks left. where do you stand to look back?

lines: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.
cards: People pin a quote above the desk, or write one line on the first page of a new notebook. A whole way of living, squeezed small enough to carry.
The Talmud tells of a man who wanted to become Jewish and dared Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot. Hillel didn't send him away.

teach.h: WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.
teach.b: Hillel's answer: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: DO AS YOU'D BE DONE BY.
teach.b: A neighbor tradition has a line close to it.
Christians read in the Gospel of Matthew, in Jesus' words: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets."

teach.h: DON'T, AND DO: SHARED, AND DIFFERENT.
teach.b: What's shared is striking. Both put a whole body of teaching into how you treat another person, and both say this is the heart of the law. The honest differences are worth keeping.
Hillel says what not to do; Matthew says what to do. And Hillel doesn't stop at the rule: he adds go and learn, so the one line opens into a lifetime of study.
Each tradition reads its own line in its own way, and neither needs the other to be the same. At the start of this long stretch on living it, you wrote a rule of life in three lines.

teach.h: KEEP THE HEART. GO AND LEARN.
teach.b: Now it gets rewritten, the way Hillel's one sentence asks: keep the heart, then keep learning.
Something to tell a friend tonight: Hillel's whole-Torah sentence ends with homework, go and learn.

how: Hillel's answer from Shabbat 31a is widely taught in Jewish schools and homes; some people write a personal rule of life, a few lines of commitments, and revisit it from time to time.

o: a motto you choose once and then never revisit
a list of laws handed down that never changes
a short rule you live by, rewritten as you grow

games.q: a life in a sentence — tap the pairs.
p: what is hateful to you, don't do
do as you'd have done to you

s: Hillel taught the whole Torah while a man stood on one foot
Shabbat 31a: 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor.'
Hillel's rule is worded as what to do for others
his says what not to do; Matthew's line says what to do.
Matthew's line says 'this is the law and the prophets'
both lines call the rule the heart of the law.

games.q: your three-line rule from months ago has one line you never managed to keep. what fits Hillel's answer?
o: keep the heart, rewrite that line, and go and learn the rest.
throw out the whole rule; it clearly didn't work.
keep it word for word; changing it would be giving up.
games.why: Hillel's one sentence ends 'go and learn.' a rule of life is meant to be kept at the heart and rewritten as you grow.

practice: Take the three-line rule you wrote at the start of this stretch, or start fresh if you never wrote one.
By hand, write it again: keep the line that held, change the one that didn't, and let one line be about how you treat other people.

wordCard.voice: Your rule: a short rule of life, in your own words, kept at the heart and rewritten as you learn.

orig.note: Aramaic: go and learn, the last words of Hillel's answer in Shabbat 31a.

carryVoice: For the road: your rule of life, short enough to say on one foot. That's your own path, gathered up.
